lead: Iowa has flooded rivers, derecho winds and long, cold winters. DryBeacon helps owners from Des Moines to Cedar Rapids get water out and dry homes the right way.
risk: river flooding, severe storms and derechos, and frozen pipes
why: The 2008 floods put much of downtown Cedar Rapids under water, and Iowa City was hit too. In 2019, the Missouri River flooded towns in western Iowa. In June 2024, the Rock and Big Sioux rivers flooded Rock Valley and other towns in northwest Iowa. FEMA has declared 41 water and storm disasters in Iowa since 2000.

Wind is the other threat. The August 2020 derecho tore through Cedar Rapids and central Iowa, damaging roofs across the region. Iowa's housing is old, with almost a quarter of homes built before 1940. Many have stone or block basements that seep in wet weather. Nebraska and Minnesota share Iowa's river risks.
image_alt: Flooded neighborhood with a temporary flood barrier along the street
image_caption: Iowa's river towns have learned to raise barriers, but water still reaches homes in big flood years.
problems: Cedar Rapids, Iowa City, western Iowa
Older homes with stone or block walls
tips: Know your flood zone; many river towns updated maps after 2008.
Keep a written list of what is stored in your basement for claims.
Seal cracks in basement walls and keep gutters clean.
Leave heat on and pipes insulated in farm outbuildings with water lines.
insurance: Iowa homeowners policies cover wind and hail, but rising river water needs a separate flood policy.

faq.q: How long does it take to dry a flooded basement in Iowa?
faq.a: Most basements take three to five days with commercial dehumidifiers and air movers. Older stone foundations and concrete can take longer. Crews check with moisture meters and stop when materials reach a dry reading.

licensing: Contractors who work in Iowa must register with the Iowa Division of Labor. Plumbing, HVAC and electrical work need state trade licenses.
